Yeah, anything other than slow a deliberate is silly. It's not a race.

Unless you're in combat, the chance to hit a squib while shooting at people who are also shooting at you is very small. Anyone who carries a gun for self-defence expends vastly large numbers of rounds while training at the range. Therefore, this is where your squib is going to happen, if at all. And you can certainly tell if you hit one. Just don't continue firing and examine the barrel.

There are two hazards here. The first is that a squib might have left a slug in the barrel, which can destroy the pistol if another round is fired before clearing it. The second is that a hang-fire can simmer for a few seconds, which can ruin your hand if you happen to be opening the action and laying your palm across the ejection port when it decides to go off.

While we are at it, a third hazard involves a normal, live round that gets hung up in the ejection port when the slide closes. If the extractor happens to hit the primer, you don't want your hand or face too close. This can happen when clearing jams in a hurry.

These risks are intrinsic to combat training. In a fight, getting the gun running again as quickly as humanly possible is the overriding concern, and that means training, and training means exposure to these risks. You can mitigate it a bit by using dummy rounds for your clearance drills, but your real-life skills will be somewhat reduced as a result.

There are basically two paths - the first is to not train this way, which is fine. When I have a gun malfunction, I stop, and act slowly and carefully to deal with it. This is bad news in a fight but I'm old and fat and too grouchy to be very tactical. The other approach is to simply accept the risk of training at that level, and to appreciate that lots of people train that way and injuries are uncommon. Be religious about wearing good eye protection and your chances of serious injury are legitimately pretty small.

On a related note, there are good tactical reasons for operating a slide by placing the weak hand over the top of it, palm down, thumb pointed back at you. Unfortunately this makes it easy - perhaps too easy - for a beginner to inadvertently allow the pistol to point to the side instead of straight downrange when manipulating it in this way. The old slingshot method - gun twisted 90 degrees to the left, weak hand thumb pointing forward, laying parallel and alongside the extended trigger finger - forces the gun to be pointed downrange and also provides some additional muscle memory to encourage the correct straightening of the trigger finger during this critical act. It's a safer, better habit, but it's not nearly as good in a fight. You just have to choose which way to go, and do your best to do it right.
